Tamworth
TAM-wurth
n. (the Staffordshire town that was the royal seat of Mercia under Offa and sank to a market town after the Danes destroyed it)
Old English Tamanweorþig, the enclosure on the river Tame; weorþig meaning an enclosed settlement.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tamworth stands where the Anker joins the Tame on the Staffordshire and Warwickshire border, and in the eighth century it was the principal residence of the kings of Mercia. Offa, who ruled from 757 to 796 and styled himself king of the whole land of the English, held his court and issued his charters there; Mercia was then the first power in Britain, with a bishopric raised at Lichfield to an archbishopric in 787 to free it from Canterbury. The Danes destroyed the place in 874, and though Aethelflaed of Mercia refortified it in 913 it never recovered its standing; the archbishopric had already been given up in 803. The collegiate church of St Editha was rebuilt after a fire in 1345. By the seventeenth century Tamworth was an ordinary market town, and it is chiefly remembered now for Peel's election address of 1834. The dictionary records the town as a case of a capital and an archbishopric both lost, and takes from it the plainest warning Scripture gives to those who reckon their security from their present eminence.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a metropolitan as an archbishop; ease as rest or quiet; to remove as to displace; a candlestick as a holder for a candle; and eminence as a rising ground or distinction.

expand to see more

METROPOLITAN, n. A bishop who presides over the other bishops of a province; an archbishop.

EASE, n. Rest; an undisturbed state; freedom from pain, disturbance or anxiety; quiet.

REMOVE, v.t. To cause to change place; to put from its place in any manner; to displace.

CANDLESTICK, n. An instrument or utensil to hold a candle, in which case it is a frame with a socket.

EMINENCE, n. Elevation; a rising ground; a hill of moderate elevation; exaltation in rank or station.

Key Scripture

Amo 6:1 — "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!"

Rev 2:5 — "Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent."

Lam 2:9 — "Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD."

Jer 17:5 — "Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Staffordshire town that was Offa's royal seat and the centre of Mercian power, with an archbishopric at Lichfield from 787, reduced by the Danes in 874 to an ordinary market town.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the pursuit of ecclesiastical rank for political convenience, and Lichfield's archbishopric is the English textbook case. Offa wanted a metropolitan of his own rather than a Kentish one, and in 787 he got the pope to raise Lichfield to an archbishopric and divide the southern province; sixteen years after his death it was quietly abolished. A see created to suit a king's frontier is not an office of Christ's appointment but a department of state, and the dictionary names the whole transaction as the subordination of church order to national interest. Jeremiah states the general rule it broke: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD” (Jer 17:5).

The second paragraph takes the town's fate as a warning and applies it where Scripture applies it, to the comfortable. Amos addresses men secure in a capital and names their security as the problem: “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations” (Amo 6:1). The risen Christ makes the same point to a church rather than a kingdom, and makes it a matter of removal: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place” (Rev 2:5). Lamentations describes what such a removal looks like from inside, when the gates are sunk into the ground and “her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more” (Lam 2:9). A royal town that lost a court, an archbishopric and its walls within forty years is a short lesson in the subject, and the dictionary enters it for that reason rather than for Peel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sha'anan (H7600), at ease or secure; Greek luchnia (G3087), a candlestick; Hebrew 'arar (H779), to curse.

expand to see more

Hebrew sha'anan (H7600) — at ease, secure, careless; “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion”, Amos 6:1.

Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; “and trust in the mountain of Samaria”, Amos 6:1.

Greek luchnia (G3087) — a lampstand, a candlestick; “will remove thy candlestick out of his place”, Revelation 2:5.

Hebrew 'arar (H779) — to curse, to execrate; “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man”, Jeremiah 17:5.

Hebrew chazon (H2377) — a vision, a revelation; “her prophets also find no vision from the LORD”, Lamentations 2:9.

Usage

"“Woe to them that are at ease in Zion” (Amo 6:1) — Offa's court at the height of Mercia."

"“will remove thy candlestick out of his place” (Rev 2:5) — the Lichfield archbishopric given up in 803."

"“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man” (Jer 17:5) — a see created to suit a king's frontier."
